metadata.title: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Specialization
metadata.subject: Economics
metadata.objective: Show opportunity costs, specialization totals, and a mutually beneficial terms-of-trade range.
misconceptions: Absolute advantage determines gains from trade
One country must lose in every trade
expectedUnderstanding: Each producer's opportunity cost comes from what must be given up.
Specialization raises total output when comparative advantage exists.
Terms of trade must lie between the two opportunity costs.
Both sides can gain, but the gains need not be equal.

primitives.text: Self-sufficient: 8 coffee + 7 cloth -> specialized: 12 coffee + 8 cloth
Specialization raises both totals: +4 coffee, +1 cloth
Mutually beneficial cloth price (coffee per cloth)

controls.label: Set the cloth price in coffee

checkpoints.title: Opportunity cost is the tradeoff
checkpoints.body: Alpha can turn 6 cloth into 12 coffee, so 1 cloth costs 2 coffee. Beta can turn 8 cloth into 4 coffee, so 1 cloth costs 0.5 coffee. The cost is what is given up, not total output.

checkpoints.title: Absolute advantage is not the test
checkpoints.body: Alpha produces more coffee and Beta produces more cloth, but the specialization decision follows lower opportunity cost. Alpha gives up less coffee per cloth? No: Alpha gives up 2 coffee per cloth, Beta only 0.5, so Beta specializes in cloth and Alpha in coffee.

checkpoints.title: Specialize and total output rises
checkpoints.body: Before specialization the total is 8 coffee + 7 cloth. After Alpha makes only coffee and Beta makes only cloth, the total is 12 coffee + 8 cloth: both totals are higher, so the total bundle has grown.

checkpoints.title: Terms of trade lie between costs
checkpoints.body: For both to gain, the price of cloth must be above Beta's 0.5-coffee cost and below Alpha's 2-coffee cost. The slider marks a price inside that band, where Beta gains from selling cloth and Alpha gains from buying it.

checkpoints.title: Both can gain without equal gains
checkpoints.body: The trade band is the set of mutually beneficial prices. Both countries can gain, so one need not lose. The exact split depends on the bargained price, so the scene does not claim the gains are equal.

narration.text: Alpha gives up 2 coffee per cloth; Beta gives up 0.5.
Absolute output is not the test; opportunity cost is.
Specialization changes total output from 8 coffee and 7 cloth to 12 and 8.
Any cloth price between 0.5 and 2 coffee can benefit both, but not equally.

fallback.text: Alpha can produce 12 coffee or 6 cloth, so 1 cloth costs Alpha 2 coffee. Beta can produce 4 coffee or 8 cloth, so 1 cloth costs Beta 0.5 coffee. Alpha has the lower opportunity cost in coffee; Beta has the lower opportunity cost in cloth. Before specialization the total is 8 coffee and 7 cloth. After Alpha specializes in coffee and Beta in cloth, the total is 12 coffee and 8 cloth, so specialization raises total output. A mutually beneficial cloth price must lie between 0.5 and 2 coffee per cloth: above 0.5, Beta gains from selling cloth; below 2, Alpha gains from buying it. Both countries can gain, but the gains need not be equal, and no country must lose.

accessibility.alt: Two producer rows with coffee and cloth bars: Alpha 12 or 6, Beta 4 or 8. Text states opportunity costs: 1 cloth costs Alpha 2 coffee and Beta 0.5. A slider marks a mutually beneficial cloth price between 0.5 and 2 coffee.
